The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, a readily accessible surrogate biomarker for insulin resistance and metabolic health, has been extensively investigated across various ethnic populations. The critical role of physical activity (PA) in enhancing insulin sensitivity has been corroborated by numerous studies. Nonetheless, the relationship between different patterns of PA and the TyG index remains ambiguous. This study seeks to elucidate the association between different PA patterns and the TyG index. Participants with complete data on TyG index, PA patterns, and other covariates from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey database (2007–2018) were included in this study. Participant characteristics across PA groups were compared using Rao-Scott chi-squared test or Kruskal–Wallis test. Multivariate linear regression models were used to assess the relationship between PA patterns and the TyG index, with subgroup analyses, interaction tests and restricted cubic spline (RCS) regression analyses conducted to explore the stability and potential nonlinearity of PA-TyG index association, respectively. A total of 16,440 participants were included, with 12,909, 164, 118, and 3249 individuals being inactive, insufficiently active, weekend warriors (WWs), and regularly active (RA), respectively. Multivariate adjusted linear regression models showed that insufficiently active adults (β = − 0.05, P = 0.3524), WWs (β = −0.01, P = 0.9129), and RA adults (β = − 0.110, P < 0.0001) all had significantly lower TyG indices compared to inactive adults. Significant difference was observed between WWs and RA adults ( P for trend < 0.0001). Stratified analyses and interact tests revealed that the PA-TyG index association in RA group was more pronounced in individuals being male, with higher education levels, and without diabetes. Additionally, a significant, non-linear, and negative relationship between weekly total PA and TyG index in non-inactive individuals was determined by RCS analysis ( P for overall < 0.001, P for nonlinearity = 0.054). Being regularly active is linked to a substantial reduction in the TyG index, whereas weekend warriors and those with insufficient activity do not experience comparable benefits. Nevertheless, the weekend warrior approach can provide a practical alternative for individuals who are unable to engage in consistent exercise. Keywords Weekend warrior Triglyceride-glucose index Physical activity NHANES Cross-sectional study Subject terms Diabetes Public health Natural Science Foundation of Guangdong Province K20113077 K20113077 K20113077 Zhang JinYe Zheng HaoNan Yu Bin issue-copyright-statement © Springer Nature Limited 2025 Introduction Physical activity (PA) is imperative for individuals of all ages to promote proper growth and development, enhance physical and cognitive function, improve sleep quality, and decrease the likelihood of chronic diseases 1 . According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 18–64 year-old adults are strongly suggested to perform 150–300 min of moderate-intensity aerobic PA, or 75–150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic PA, or an equivalent combination of both throughout the week for the harvest of substantial health benefits 2 . In recent years, since leisure time physical activity on weekends may be a more convenient option for many people, an increasing number of individuals have chosen to focus on 1 or 2 physical activities per week, known as “Weekend Warriors” (WWs) 3 . A large prospective cohort study suggested that individuals who engage in active physical activity patterns, whether weekend warriors or regular exercisers have lower all-cause and cause-specific mortality rates than inactive individuals do 4 . However, it is unclear whether concentrating on physical activity over one or two days (known as the weekend warrior pattern) can achieve the same benefits as exercising regularly. Insulin resistance (IR) has been proved to correlate with increased risks of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, etc., while PA has been demonstrated to be one of the most reliable strategies to alleviate IR 5 . The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is a simple, convenient, and low-cost marker of IR that does not require insulin quantification 6 – 8 . This index can be calculated simply by fasting triglycerides and fasting glucose in routine biochemical tests and is not restricted by insulin therapy 9 . In recent years, several studies have shown that the TyG index can be used to identify individuals at risk for developing diabetes in the future and presents is associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD), stroke, depression, and sleep disorders 10 – 14 . However, whether the TyG index, an index closely related to health, can be improved by physical activity (PA) is unknown. Also, it is unclear whether there is a correlation between PA patterns and the TyG index, and whether the benefits of different PA patterns are similar. Therefore, we investigated the relationship between PA patterns and the TyG index via a cross-sectional study of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cohort. This study aimed to increase of the positive impact of exercise patterns on the TyG index and to provide recommendations for adopting different activity patterns to mitigate the risk of various diseases.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: Physical activity (PA) enhances insulin sensitivity, thereby alleviating insulin resistance (IR). The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index serves as a readily accessible surrogate biomarker for IR, calculated from fasting triglycerides and glucose. PA directly normalizes glycogen synthesis and IR, reduces hepatic lipid content and de novo lipogenesis through interactions among liver, skeletal muscle, and adipose tissue. Indirectly, PA increases energy expenditure, improves body composition, reduces adipose tissue inflammation and liver ectopic lipid deposition, and enhances skeletal muscle metabolic capacity.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: Regularly active (RA) adults exhibited significantly lower triglyceride-glucose (TyG) indices (β = -0.110, P < 0.0001) compared to inactive adults, with RA individuals demonstrating a significantly lower TyG index than Weekend Warriors (WWs) (P for trend < 0.0001). In contrast, insufficiently active adults (β = -0.05, P = 0.3524) and WWs (β = -0.01, P = 0.9129) did not experience comparable benefits; specifically, WWs were associated with a notable TyG index increase when compared to the regularly active group, and did not achieve significant TyG index reduction comparable to RA. Physical activity (PA) patterns were classified by total MVPA levels, with insufficiently active at 120 min, WWs at 290 min, and RA at 540 min. A significant, non-linear, and negative relationship was observed between weekly total PA and the TyG index in non-inactive individuals (P for overall < 0.001), where the TyG index gradually decreased as total PA increased. Even PA not meeting recommended standards was associated with a lower TyG index compared to inactivity. Research suggests a minimum exercise threshold (e.g., 1200-1600 kcal/week or moderate-intensity PA 3-5 times/week) is crucial for metabolic changes. For instance, at least 40-45 minutes per session, three times a week over 12 weeks, improved hepatic steatosis, implying that two sessions (characteristic of WWs) might be insufficient. The quantity and frequency of PA are more critical for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes than mode or intensity.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The association between physical activity (PA) and the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, particularly in the regularly active (RA) group, was more pronounced in males, individuals with higher education levels, and those without diabetes (all P interaction < 0.05). Notably, only RA individuals experienced a significant TyG index reduction, whereas Weekend Warriors (WWs) did not achieve comparable benefits. Furthermore, no significant or nonlinear associations between total PA per week and the TyG index were observed in the insufficiently active and WWs subgroups. Similarly, no significant or linear relationship was found between weekly sedentary time and the TyG index in inactive, insufficiently active, and WWs subgroups. Alarmingly, individuals classified as WWs demonstrated a significantly higher likelihood of developing metabolic syndrome compared to those in the RA group (OR = 1.29, 95% CI 1.02–1.65).

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: US adults aged 18-64 years (based on NHANES 2007–2018 data, N=16,440), including individuals unable to engage in regular exercise, patients with type 2 diabetes, obese women, and Chinese type 2 diabetes patients with a BMI lower than 35 kg/m^2. Specific associations were more pronounced in males, individuals with higher education levels, and those without diabetes.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Regular physical activity (PA) is crucial for improving insulin sensitivity and managing the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, thereby alleviating insulin resistance and enhancing overall metabolic health. This translates to a decreased likelihood of chronic diseases such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease (CVD), metabolic syndrome, obesity, stroke, depression, and sleep disorders. The TyG index itself is a valuable biomarker for the onset, progression, and prognosis of various conditions, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, sarcopenia, malignancies, and for predicting metabolic syndrome and hypogonadism. Maintaining an optimal TyG index through PA is also associated with a reduced risk of atherosclerosis, lower all-cause, cardiovascular disease, and cancer mortality rates, improved body composition (e.g., decreased visceral adiposity index, combating fat accumulation), and optimized glycemic control, particularly beneficial for managing obesity and improving hepatic steatosis.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Regular physical activity (PA) confers a significant protective benefit against insulin resistance (IR) and related metabolic and chronic diseases, evidenced by a substantial reduction in the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index. The TyG index serves as a reliable diagnostic and prognostic marker for identifying individuals at risk for developing future diabetes, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, and other IR-related conditions. While the "Weekend Warrior" (WWs) pattern can offer some protective benefits for individuals with limited time, it does not achieve comparable TyG index reductions to regular activity and is associated with a notably higher risk (OR = 1.29) of developing metabolic syndrome when compared to regularly active individuals. Thus, while any activity is better than none, regular and consistent PA offers superior protective health outcomes.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index is considered a reliable, readily accessible, simple, convenient, and low-cost surrogate biomarker for insulin resistance (IR) and metabolic health. It is derived from enzymatically determined fasting triglycerides and fasting glucose, measured by automated biochemistry analysers, and does not require insulin quantification or is restricted by insulin therapy. The TyG index has been shown to be superior to HOMA-IR in predicting metabolic syndrome and hypogonadism, identifying IR in Chinese type 2 diabetes patients (BMI < 35 kg/m^2), and evaluating the odds of atherosclerosis. While the study ensured representativeness by using appropriate NHANES sample weights, strata, and cluster variables, it has limitations, including its cross-sectional design preventing causal inference, consideration of limited variables, potential bias from self-reported physical activity data, and the lack of accounting for dietary habits or calorie intake. The text does not provide an explicit assessment of the biomarker's sensitivity or specific reliability beyond these comparisons.
